title: OpenAI to cut Cursor's model access on Nov 12 after SpaceX takeover closes
subtitle: OpenAI invoked a change-of-ownership clause and cited past xAI and Twitter terms-of-service violations as its reason for ending the contract at the latest allowed date.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI notified SpaceX that it will wind down the contract providing OpenAI models to Cursor, the AI coding platform SpaceX finished acquiring earlier in August in a $60 billion stock deal. The shut-off is set for November 12, 2026 — the latest date the change-of-ownership provision in the Cursor contract allows. In its published note, OpenAI wrote that it 'cannot be confident SpaceX will use OpenAI's technology within its terms of service,' citing prior contract disputes with both Twitter and xAI as precedent. Any new OpenAI models released between now and November 12 will not be available inside Cursor.

The practical bite is real: on some usage estimates, OpenAI's GPT-5.6 line has been the most-selected model inside Cursor since its July rollout. Cursor's tab-completion and agent modes will still work — they can route to Anthropic's Claude, xAI's Grok, Google's Gemini and the growing bench of open-weight coding models — but for teams that standardized on GPT-5.6 as the deep-refactor default, November means a forced migration. Cursor itself pivots into an odd position: an Elon Musk-owned coding tool whose in-house Grok models compete with the OpenAI models its users prefer.

The move is the second high-profile contractual break of the SpaceX-Cursor era. In April, when the acquisition was announced, Anthropic pre-emptively narrowed the API terms that had let Cursor resell Claude, forcing Cursor onto a new commercial tier. OpenAI now walks the same path with a longer runway. Both companies frame it as terms-of-service enforcement; Musk's camp frames it as a coordinated squeeze on a competitor's coding stack. Either reading, the direction is the same — frontier-lab model access is no longer a neutral utility that flows to whichever coding IDE the developer picks; it is an alignment decision made lab by lab.

For learners: if your daily workflow depends on a specific model reachable through a third-party wrapper — an IDE plugin, a chat wrapper, a workflow tool — you have a supply-chain risk that has nothing to do with the model's quality. It is worth knowing which lab you are ultimately talking to, whether the wrapper has a direct commercial agreement, and what your fallback looks like if that agreement gets pulled. In this cycle, that answer changes on the order of once a quarter.
